summary: The article examines whether the post-2023 employment boom in green energy is durable or a bubble. It cites IRENA data, company expansions, government incentives, new skill demands, international growth, automation fears, and consumer and corporate pressure. It concludes that policy, consumer expectations and technology suggest the green job market is resilient and likely to keep growing.
one_line: An analysis of green energy job growth after 2023 concludes the boom looks resilient, driven by policy, consumer demand and infrastructure, despite automation concerns.
key_facts: On September 5th, 2023, the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) released a report saying renewable energy was the fastest-growing energy source globally, accounting for two-thirds of new power added to the world's grids.
Solarize Inc., led by CEO Arnold Wainwright, invested heavily in solar technologies and had quadrupled its workforce by late 2023.
As of October 2023, several governments launched incentives to bolster renewable energy companies, tied to Green New Deal propositions.
ElectraWind, led by CEO Maria Chen, expanded to new regions by end of 2023 and hired thousands of technicians, engineers and support staff for wind farms.
Professor Johnathan Ellery of the Green Tech Institute said "Upskilling is not just a buzzword; it's an economic imperative" as fossil fuel jobs wane.

Roles in project management, environmental law and sustainable supply chain management have emerged as in-demand green jobs, and educators and industry leaders began talks in late 2023 to bridge the 'green skills gap'.
Kenya's solar power initiatives have created a boom in urban and rural employment since late 2023, and Scandinavia is exporting green expertise.
Dr. Alfred Hopkins, a technology ethicist, warned at a December 2023 symposium that over-reliance on automated technologies could neutralize job growth in renewables.
GreenFuture Enterprises CEO Laura Gilbert declared that to be competitive, "we have we have to be green," driving new roles in environmental auditing and sustainability reporting.
Market analyst Benjamin Sato projected that consumer demand will continue to heavily influence corporate strategy, with sustainability at the helm.
As reported in February 2024, the number of vocational programs and academic degrees in environmental studies and sustainability has multiplied.
Green infrastructure development is creating jobs in city planning, construction and grid modernization, benefiting urban planners and civil engineers.
